items.title: Motivation in the Public Sector: Bureaucratic dimensions’ relation to public servants’ intrinsic motivation in context of self-determination and age
items.abstract: Public servants’ intrinsic motivation—‘their experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work’—is an important correlate of performance (Wright 2004; Cerasoli et al. 2014; Sansone & Harackiewicz 2000) and well-being (Ryan & Deci 2000). Conversely, a lack of intrinsic motivation inhibits the creativity (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Houtgraaf et al. 2021; Houtgraaf et al. 2023) and productivity (Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013) required to provide the effective, user-centered policies/services that citizens need and demand (Clarke et al. 2007; Van Thiel 2017; Torfing 2016). Furthermore, inadequate motivation diminishes public servants’ experienced wellbeing (Barret-Cheetham et al. 2016; Borst 2018) and is associated with dissatisfaction, boreout, burnout, turnover and part-time work in the public sector (Kim 2018; Borst & Knies 2023; Stazyk et al. 2011). Adequate levels of intrinsic motivation are thus of central importance for both workforce performance, well-being and retention. Meanwhile, both practitioners and academics voice that captivating and retaining public servants is increasingly becoming a challenge—especially with more junior public servants. In general, attracting and retaining an intrinsically motivated workforce appears difficult due to numerous developments in both the nature of work and the nature of employees (Davidesque et al. 2020; Twenge et al. 2010; Cahill et al. 2012). In the public sector too, sustainable employment is of growing concern, illustrated by efforts to understand and safeguard public servants’ well-being, performance and retention (Van der Meer et al. 2022; Borst & Knies 2023; Johari et al. 2019). The challenges of captivating and retaining seems especially true for employees from more recent generations—or at least of younger age (Schröder 2023)—that are argued to have different and more pronounced expectations and preferences relating to work (Waworuntu et al. 2022). In the Netherlands, for example, the translated ‘captivate and bind’ programs sprout throughout the public sector in an alarmed effort to retain (junior) public servants (Binnenlands Bestuur 2024). However, our knowledge regarding intrinsic motivation amidst bureaucratic constraints falls short on two major accounts. Firstly, insight is lacking on whether a lack of intrinsic motivation is an issue in the public sector as a result of bureaucratic constraints and through what mechanisms this would or would not occur. On the one hand, bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization arguably have several negative effects that relate to a lack of intrinsic motivation (Giauque et al. 2012; George et al. 2021; Lavigna 2013; Serhan et al. 2018). On the other hand, such bureaucratic constraints might not lead to amotivation as public servants’ motivation is argued to be a relatively stable concept (Baldwin 1990; Houtgraaf & Ropes in press) and because public servants’ argued idiosyncratic personality may actually lead them to value bureaucratic elements (Leisha & DeHart-Davis 2007; Merton 1940; Bozeman & Rainey 1998). Applying Self-Determination Theory and assessing whether bureaucratic constraints as forms of external locus of control diminish public servants’ sense of autonomy and competence and thereby lead to amotivation (Ryan & Deci 2000, see also Ekval 1996) would provide insight on underlying mechanisms but has not been applied. Secondly, insight is lacking on the role of age/generation, despite evidence pointing towards a significant moderating function. Millennials and more recent generations are argued to assign particular value to elements of autonomy and positive hierarchical feedback relating to competence in their work (Waworuntu et al. 2022), which appears at odds with bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization typically present in the public sector that may stifle such senses of autonomy and competence (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000; Ekval 1996). Moreover, recent findings dispute that such differences relating to work motivation and preferences are a result of generational differences but a function of age (Schröder 2023). In short, insight is lacking on whether and why bureaucratic constraints relate to amotivation, what role age/generation plays and thus what strategies and tactics to employ in order to captivate and retain public servants—especially junior ones. Therefore, the goal of this study was to scrutinize whether and how bureaucratic dimensions relate to public servants’ intrinsic motivation whilst paying particular attention to self-determination as an underlying mechanism and the role of age. To these ends, several analyses are conducted on cross-sectional data from 1158 public servants working in a range of Dutch public sector organizations to answer the research question: ‘Through which mechanisms do levels of public servants’ intrinsic motivation correlate with the presence of bureaucratic dimensions, taking into account age?’. Scrutinizing these mechanisms allowed for detailed insights in mechanisms of intrinsic motivation and how to safeguard it in the public sector context, especially among specific age groups. The ensuing results provide public sector practitioners, managers, HR-departments and training organizations with avenues on whether and how to effectively counter adverse effects of bureaucratic dimensions on public servants’ motivation in order to captivate and retain public servants’ and in turn improve their performance, wellbeing and sustainable employment. MOTIVATION AMIDST BUREAUCRATIC CONSTRAINTS Intrinsic motivation and Self-Determination Theory Intrinsic motivation encompasses an experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work that stems from the employee itself, instead of external factors (Wright 2004; Ryan & Deci 2000; Li et al. 2015). According to Self-Determination Theory, the central characteristic of intrinsic motivation is that it stems from an internal locus of control whereby the individual experiences a control over its own actions and outcomes, instead of an external locus of control whereby the individual experiences that its actions and outcomes are determined by external factors such as managers or rules (Deci & Ryan 1985; Li et al. 2015). In more detail, according to Self-Determination Theory, senses of autonomy, competence and relatedness are essential psychological needs that can be satisfied or frustrated and thus determine the degree of an internal locus of control and experience of intrinsic motivation: the individual has to perceive itself as an autonomous actor that is able and capable of acting in correspondence with its values and goals (Chen et al. 2015; Deci & Ryan 1985). External locus of control, however, may lead to a lack of perceived internal locus of control, hampering intrinsic motivation (Bénabou & Tirole 2003; Deci and Ryan 1985) and leading to amotivation whereby the enjoyment, interest and satisfaction of work becomes increasingly absent (Howard et al., 2016). In general, intrinsic motivation is perceived as beneficial for performance and well-being (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Ryan & Deci 2000; Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013), which results in the reasoning that an impairing external locus of control that may hamper employees’ intrinsic motivation ought to be avoided. When assessing intrinsic motivation, it is important to determine whether the concept is approached as an attitude or a state, depending on the goal and timeline of assessment. If considered an attitude, intrinsic motivation is assessed based on an individual’s recall over a longer period of time based on the remembering-self, thereby leading to a more average and stable assessment of the level of intrinsic motivation, whereas if considered a state, intrinsic motivation is assessed on based on an individual’s experience in the current moment based on the experiencing-self, thereby leading to accurate but momentarily and fluctuating assessments of levels of intrinsic motivation (Kahneman & Riis 2005). As the goal of this study concerns assessing how individuals recall their work contexts and attitudes in general and on average in order to assess relations, intrinsic motivation is approached and measured as an attitude in this study (Lee & Choi 2003). Formalization as external locus of control Formalization—the degree to which work related processes and interactions are generally governed by formal rules, standard policies and procedures (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000)—can be perceived as representing external locus of control that may hamper public servants’ intrinsic motivation. Formalization is a typical bureaucratic dimension of mechanistic organizations (Brown 2014) and although public sector reforms have aimed at reduction of formalization (Van Thiel 2001), public sector organizations are characterized as featuring at least certain levels of formalization (Borins 2010; Boyne 2002; Boye et al. 2022; Houtgraaf et al. 2023). The object of such bureaucratic principles as expressed in formalization is to achieve stability, standardization and to avoid flexibility and change (Ekval 1996) by controlling employee behavior (Hirst et al. 2009). As such, formalization is a clear example of external locus of control that may hamper intrinsic motivation. Arguably, the underlying mechanisms are twofold. On the one hand, the rules and procedures imposed by formalization may frustrate a sense of autonomy as the individual might not be able to act as it would without these external controls (Hirst et al. 2009). On the other hand, formalization its rules and procedures are related to passive, rule-bound and anxious behavior to stay inside established boundaries (Ekval 1996), which may frustrate a sense of competence as the individual might feel less capable and efficacious in conducting work as a result of the external controls (Au 2015). items.title: Needs and Requirements for a chatbot supporting student mental well-being
items.abstract: Going to university has various implications for many students, like leaving home, becoming independent, having to look for new friendships, and creating a new routine. These changes can impact the mental well-being of students who sometimes find themselves alone to deal with a general malaise. Poor student mental well-being is a big problem in the Netherlands and, in a research conducted by Dopmeijer et al. (2021) for the “Ministerie van Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap” [In English: Ministry of Education, Culture and Science] it was found that more than half of students have symptoms related to poor student mental well-being. The consequences associated with it are for example stress, anxiety, sadness, loneliness (Dopmeijer et al., 2021), and in some cases dropping out of school (Grové, 2021). However, students might have difficulty seeking the help of a professional because they are not fully aware of the meaning of their symptoms (Eisenberg, Golberstein, & Gollust, 2007), they do not trust professional support due to confidentiality (Westberg et al., 2022) and because of fear of stigma from families, friends, and peers (Ferrie, Miller, & Hunter, 2020; Westberg et al., 2022). In the long run, the lack of support might lead to more serious mental health issues. As a preventive measure, chatbots can be of help. A chatbot is a computer program designed to respond with conversational or informational replies to verbal or written message from users (Dictionary, n.d.). Students can talk to a chatbot 24/7, so they can always have someone to talk to that can act, for instance, as a companion and give advice. In literature, it was found that with chatbots students are less afraid of being stigmatised due to the anonymity they perceive when sharing personal information (Pesonen, 2021). Additionally, the new generations are used to technology and they are more inclined to accept a chatbot as support (Koulouri, Macredie, & Olakitan, 2022). Accordingly, in the project “What’s BOThering You?”, researchers from different universities are planning to develop a chatbot that can support students in improving their mental well-being. This chatbot will be a supplement and not a replacement for the student counsellors. Nonetheless, this chatbot needs to be developed according to the needs and requirements of the students to ensure chatbot’s acceptance and effectiveness. To do so, a user-centred design (UCD) approach is used. This means taking into consideration the users’ needs, requirements, opinions and characteristics throughout the whole development of the technology (ISO 9241-210, 2019, under human-centred design). By also involving stakeholders who are affected by the topic of student mental well-being, the later implementation of the chatbot can also be facilitated. In this study, we want to explore the needs and requirements of the students, from the point of view of the student counsellors and the students. This to begin to have an idea about our target group and about how universities support students in their mental well-being. Finally, there is still lack of clarity on the process of translation from needs to requirements and how this can be optimised, in particular for chatbot for mental well-being (Koulouri et al., 2022). items.title: On the Interplay of Motivational Characteristics and Academic Achievement: The Role of Need for Cognition
items.abstract: While intelligence and motivational variables are well-established predictors of academic achievement, Need for Cognition (NFC), the stable intrinsic motivation to engage in and enjoy challenging intellectual activity, has not yet been considered comprehensively in this field, especially not longitudinally. By applying latent change score modeling, we examined the incremental value of NFC, considering well-established motivational constructs and prior achievement in the prediction of academic achievement across different subjects in a longitudinal approach across two time points in a sample of secondary school students ([Formula: see text] = 271, [Formula: see text] = 255). Correlations of NFC with grades were comparable to those of established predictors. NFC incrementally predicted academic achievement over and above prior achievement and ability self-concept. A mutual influence of NFC and academic achievement was found pointing to skill development as well as self-enhancement processes taking place in this interplay. Consequently, we propose to include NFC in models for the comprehensive explanation of academic achievement in school.

items.title: OSINT Research Studios: A Flexible Crowdsourcing Framework to Scale Up Open Source Intelligence Investigations
items.abstract: Open Source Intelligence (OSINT) investigations, which rely entirely on publicly available data such as social media, play an increasingly important role in solving crimes and holding governments accountable. The growing volume of data and complex nature of tasks, however, means there is a pressing need to scale and speed up OSINT investigations. Expert-led crowdsourcing approaches show promise but tend to either focus on narrow tasks or domains or require resource-intense, long-term relationships between expert investigators and crowds. We address this gap by providing a flexible framework that enables investigators across domains to enlist crowdsourced support for the discovery and verification of OSINT. We use a design-based research (DBR) approach to develop OSINT Research Studios (ORS), a sociotechnical system in which novice crowds are trained to support professional investigators with complex OSINT investigations. Through our qualitative evaluation, we found that ORS facilitates ethical and effective OSINT investigations across multiple domains. We also discuss broader implications of expert-crowd collaboration and opportunities for future work.

items.title: Predictive factors of occupational stress in operating theatre nurses: scoping review
items.abstract: Objective: To map the predictive factors of occupational stress in operating theatre nurses. Background: Occupational stress manifests itself through psychological and psychological changes associated with work. High exposure to stress by nurses leads to physical and psychological exhaustion, more distant behaviour and feelings of powerlessness and inadequacy. The operating theatre is considered a stressful hospital service where continuous relationships are established in a closed environment. The perioperative nurse acts as an active link with the organisation's risk management and occupational health, reducing the incidence of occupational stress. Material and methods: A Scoping Review will be carried out according to the methodology of The Joanna Briggs Institute (2020), using the PCC mnemonic (Population: nurses; Concept: predictive factors of occupational stress; Context: OR). Studies will be included in English, Spanish and Portuguese, between 2013 and 2023, in the LILACS (via the Virtual Health Library), SciELO, CINAHL Complete and WorldCat databases. Studies carried out in paediatric operating theatres and emergency operating theatres will be excluded. The selection of articles will be presented in a PRISMA-ScR flowchart (2018). The extracted data will be presented in a table. Expected results: We hope to identify the predictive factors of occupational stress in operating theatre nurses. Potential implications for practice: This study is expected to alert organisations to the issue under study and promote intervention by operating theatre nurses in order to reduce the prevalence of occupational stress and its consequences.

items.title: Professional Practices in Occupational Therapy, Health and Work: a protocol for a scoping review
items.abstract: Occupational Health is a field of intersectoral knowledge and practices that aims to promote and protect health, prevent injuries, as well as assist and rehabilitate workers who become ill as a result of production processes. In this context, Occupational Therapy, as one of the health professions, works directly with this population, with employing institutions and public policies in the field. Objective: This study aim to map and characterize the state of the art of scientific productions on the practice of Occupational Therapy in health and work. Methodology: This is a bibliographic scoping review, which follows the steps proposed by the Joanna Briggs Institute protocol and the extension for Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews (PRISMA-ScR) scoping reviews. It will be carried out in the first half of 2024, with the support of Rayyan software. All steps performed will be reported in the scope review. To survey the studies, the databases PubMed, BVS, CINAHL, Scielo and Scopus will be used, for the following descriptors: Occupational Therapy, health, work, practices and using their variants for each keyword. At the end of the research, the aim is to highlight the plurality of practices in this field and identify possible gaps to promote future investigations.

items.title: Promoting plant-based alternatives
items.abstract: Obesity is a major risk factor for developing diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, or cancer, resulting in 4.7 million premature deaths each year (WHO, 2023). Previous studies have shown that eating red meat is associated with a higher body mass index (Key et al., 2006; Rouhani et al., 2014). A promising approach to reducing meat consumption is to provide comparable alternatives (Font-i-Furnols, 2023). Therefore, the current study will investigate how we can decrease the consumption of red meat by promoting plant-based alternatives. However, studies have shown that people show strong resistance to persuasive attempts to change one's food choices (Terrien, 2018). Despite the growing popularity of plant-based diets, meat continues to be a central part of many people's diets, based on personal and social factors such as taste, identity, and culture (Terrien, 2018; Keller, 2019). Self-Determination Theory (SDT; Ryan & Deci, 2017) suggests that humans have three basic psychological needs: Autonomy, competence, and relatedness. SDT predicts that fulfilling these needs fosters intrinsic motivation to perform a certain behavior. In the current study, we focus on message characteristics that can increase autonomy. We will test whether using autonomy-supportive communication and acknowledging resistance can increase the intention to consume plant-based alternatives and decrease the intention to consume red meat.

items.title: Psycho-emotional status of nurses related to their work conditions
items.abstract: Background: Occupational nursing plays a crucial role in the prevention of occupational diseases and the promotion of the comprehensive well-being of workers. However, despite its importance, there is growing concern about the mental health of nurses, showing high levels of work stress, burnout, and other emotional problems, which underlines the urgent need to address this situation to guarantee well-being of nursing staff and the quality of patient care. Objective: to make an exhaustive description of the main psycho-emotional problems of nurses related to their work activity. Search: A scoping review was carried out that includes reviews and meta-analyses in English, Spanish, Portuguese and Italian with at least 50% of the included studies published from 2018 onwards that include only nurses and relate working conditions to pisco-emotional problems. The search engines were Embase, Medline, Cinahl, PsycINFO, SCI-EXPANDED, SSCI, Scopus, Scielo, LILACS, BDENF. After applying the inclusion criteria, eliminating duplicates, and screening the articles by title and abstract and subsequently reading the full articles, a total of 9 articles remained. Discussion: Various factors in the work environment of nurses, such as workload, workplace violence, lack of preparation, isolation of patients during the pandemic, and lack of material and human resources, contribute to problems emotional and psychological in nurses. These problems include thoughts of fear, worry, and unpreparedness, as well as feelings of loneliness, frustration, sadness, and anger. They may experience symptoms such as emotional exhaustion, job dissatisfaction, anxiety, depression, sleep disorders, and unresolved grief. These problems affect not only individual nurses, but also their ability to provide quality care to patients and generate additional costs for healthcare institutions. Keywords Occupational health, Nursing, Psycho-emotional state, Working conditions

items.title: Psychological Engagement Theory
items.abstract: Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2022. Psychological Engagement Theory. Ávila Murallas Publicaciones Internacionales, Edición Especial 2022. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/ubvjh Psychological Engagement Theory, introduced by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad in 2022, emerged from the need to understand how psychological engagement can impact individual performance and well-being. In an increasingly complex world, emotional and cognitive engagement in various aspects of life is crucial for achieving optimal outcomes. This theory provides guidance on how individuals can enhance their engagement in work, education, and social interactions to achieve better well-being and performance. Definition and Basic Concepts Psychological Engagement Theory defines psychological engagement as a state where individuals are emotionally and cognitively connected to a task, activity, or relationship. The basic concept of this theory is that high engagement involves full attention, enthusiasm, and dedication to what one is doing. The theory emphasizes that good psychological engagement not only boosts productivity and performance but also leads to greater emotional satisfaction and well-being. Underlying Phenomena The theory is based on the phenomenon that many individuals often feel disconnected or less engaged in their daily work or activities. This lack of engagement can lead to stress, decreased performance, and dissatisfaction. For instance, in the workplace, disengaged employees tend to have lower productivity and are more susceptible to burnout. This phenomenon highlights the importance of increasing psychological engagement to create a productive and fulfilling environment. Working Principles The working principles of Psychological Engagement Theory involve several key steps. First, it is important to create a supportive and motivating environment. Second, ensuring that individuals feel valued and recognized for their contributions is crucial. Third, providing appropriate challenges and opportunities for personal and professional growth is essential. The theory also emphasizes the importance of effective communication and constructive feedback to enhance psychological engagement. Indicators Key indicators of this theory include levels of emotional and cognitive engagement, job satisfaction, and individual performance. Other indicators include a sense of belonging, intrinsic motivation, and the quality of interpersonal relationships. Measuring these indicators can be done through engagement surveys, interviews, and behavioral observations in various contexts. These indicators help evaluate how engaged and committed individuals feel towards their tasks or activities. Operational Variables Operational variables of Psychological Engagement Theory include measuring levels of emotional engagement, the quality of feedback, and a sense of belonging. These variables can be measured through surveys, self-assessments, and performance data analysis. This data provides insights into how individuals are psychologically engaged and how interventions can be designed to enhance this engagement. Application Areas The theory can be applied in various fields such as Human Resource Management (HRM), Psychology, Education, Social Communication, and Health. In HRM, the theory helps develop programs that boost employee engagement and improve job performance. In Psychology, the theory is useful for understanding how individuals can enhance their engagement in various aspects of life to achieve better well-being. In Education, the theory supports the development of curricula that promote student engagement in the learning process. In Social Communication, the theory guides strategies to increase community engagement in social and community activities. In Health, the theory aids in designing programs that encourage patient engagement in their healthcare to improve health outcomes. Determining Factors The success of applying this theory is determined by several key factors. Support from the social and organizational environment is crucial to create conditions that foster psychological engagement. Additionally, effective communication, constructive feedback, and opportunities for growth are key factors. Success is also influenced by individuals' ability to utilize available resources and opportunities to enhance their engagement. Implementation and Strategies Implementing this theory requires a structured and ongoing approach. The first step is to identify the need for psychological engagement and develop appropriate programs. Effective strategies include providing training on the importance of engagement, developing policies that support psychological engagement, and creating mechanisms for feedback and evaluation. Continuous evaluation and adjustment of strategies based on individual feedback are vital to ensure long-term success. Supporting and Hindering Challenges Challenges in applying this theory include resistance to change, a lack of understanding of the importance of psychological engagement, and limited resources to develop and implement engagement programs. However, with strong support from the social and organizational environment, as well as ongoing education, these challenges can be overcome. Success also depends on the ability to create environments that support individual engagement and adaptation, and the ability to manage conflicts and barriers that may arise in the process of developing psychological engagement. Conclusion Psychological Engagement Theory emphasizes the importance of psychological engagement in achieving optimal well-being and performance. The theory provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and facilitating psychological engagement in various fields. With proper implementation, this theory can help individuals and organizations increase their engagement, better face challenges, and create positive impacts on well-being and performance. items.abstract: Rachmad, Yoesoep Edhie. 2022. Psychological Innovation Theory. Hoorn Gouden Eeuw Boek Internationale Uitgeverij, Speciale Editie 2022. https://doi.org/10.17605/osf.io/2sq7x Psychological Innovation Theory, introduced by Yoesoep Edhie Rachmad in 2022, emerged from the need to understand how innovation can be driven through psychological approaches. In a constantly changing and challenging world, innovation is key to organizational success and sustainability. This theory was developed to provide guidance on how individuals and organizations can create environments that foster creativity and innovation through the understanding and management of psychological factors. Definition and Basic Concepts Psychological Innovation Theory defines psychological innovation as the process by which individuals and groups use psychological insights to create new ideas and effective solutions. The basic concept of this theory is that understanding motivation, emotions, and cognition can be used to drive creativity and find new approaches to problems. The theory emphasizes the importance of internal factors such as self-confidence, intrinsic motivation, and openness to new experiences in fostering innovation. Underlying Phenomena The theory is based on the phenomenon that many organizations face barriers to fostering innovation due to a lack of understanding of the psychological factors underlying creativity. For example, fear of failure, lack of emotional support, and a culture that does not support risk-taking can hinder innovation. This phenomenon shows that innovation relies not only on technical skills but also on the ability to create a psychologically supportive environment. When individuals feel safe to experiment and share ideas, they are more likely to produce innovative solutions. Working Principles The working principles of Psychological Innovation Theory involve several key steps. First, it is important to create a supportive psychological environment where individuals feel safe to take risks and experiment. Second, providing emotional support and motivation is crucial to encourage engagement and creativity. Third, developing openness to new experiences and different perspectives is essential. The theory also emphasizes the importance of self-reflection and learning from failure as part of the innovation process. Indicators Key indicators of this theory include the level of individual and team creativity, the number of new ideas generated, and the success of innovation implementation. Other indicators include the level of openness to new experiences, intrinsic motivation, and job satisfaction. These indicators can be measured through surveys, interviews, and analysis of work outcomes in various contexts. They help evaluate how well individuals and organizations succeed in fostering innovation through psychological approaches. Operational Variables Operational variables of Psychological Innovation Theory include measuring levels of creativity, quality of emotional support, and openness to new experiences. These variables can be measured through surveys, self-assessments, and performance data analysis. This data provides insights into how psychological factors influence the innovation process and how interventions can be designed to enhance creativity and innovation. Application Areas The theory can be applied in various fields such as Human Resource Management (HRM), Psychology, Education, Social Communication, and Health. In HRM, the theory helps develop programs that increase employee creativity and innovation. In Psychology, it is useful for understanding how psychological factors can be used to drive innovation. In Education, the theory supports the development of curricula that promote creativity and innovative thinking among students. In Social Communication, the theory guides strategies to enhance engagement and innovation within communities. In Health, the theory helps design programs that support innovation in care and health management. Determining Factors The success of applying this theory is determined by several key factors. Support from leaders and management is crucial for creating an environment that supports innovation. Additionally, adequate training and resources to develop creative skills are essential. Success also depends on the ability to use self-reflection and learning from failure as part of the innovation process. Implementation and Strategies Implementing this theory requires a structured and ongoing approach. The first step is identifying the needs and barriers to innovation within the organization and developing appropriate programs. Effective strategies include providing training on creativity and innovation, developing policies that support experimentation and risk-taking, and creating mechanisms for feedback and evaluation. Continuous evaluation and adjustment of strategies based on feedback from individuals are critical for ensuring long-term success. Supporting and Hindering Challenges Challenges in applying this theory include resistance to change, lack of understanding of the importance of psychological factors in innovation, and limited resources to develop and implement innovation programs. However, with strong support from leaders and a supportive organizational culture, along with ongoing education, these challenges can be overcome. Success also relies on the ability to create an environment that fosters individual engagement and innovation, as well as the ability to manage conflicts and barriers that may arise in the innovation process. Conclusion Psychological Innovation Theory emphasizes the importance of psychological factors in driving creativity and innovation. The theory provides a comprehensive framework for understanding and facilitating the innovation process across various fields. With proper application, this theory can help individuals and organizations enhance their ability to innovate, better face challenges, and create a positive impact on performance and well-being. items.title: Public Sector Motivation: Bureaucratic dimensions’ relation to public servants’ intrinsic motivation in context of self-determination and age
items.abstract: Public servants’ intrinsic motivation—‘their experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work’—is an important correlate of performance (Wright 2004; Cerasoli et al. 2014; Sansone & Harackiewicz 2000) and well-being (Ryan & Deci 2000). Conversely, a lack of intrinsic motivation inhibits the creativity (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Houtgraaf et al. 2021; Houtgraaf et al. 2023) and productivity (Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013) required to provide the effective, user-centered policies/services that citizens need and demand (Clarke et al. 2007; Van Thiel 2017; Torfing 2016). Furthermore, inadequate motivation diminishes public servants’ experienced wellbeing (Barret-Cheetham et al. 2016; Borst 2018) and is associated with dissatisfaction, boreout, burnout, turnover and part-time work in the public sector (Kim 2018; Borst & Knies 2023; Stazyk et al. 2011). Adequate levels of intrinsic motivation are thus of central importance for both workforce performance, well-being and retention. Meanwhile, both practitioners and academics voice that captivating and retaining public servants is increasingly becoming a challenge—especially with more junior public servants. In general, attracting and retaining an intrinsically motivated workforce appears difficult due to numerous developments in both the nature of work and the nature of employees (Davidesque et al. 2020; Twenge et al. 2010; Cahill et al. 2012). In the public sector too, sustainable employment is of growing concern, illustrated by efforts to understand and safeguard public servants’ well-being, performance and retention (Van der Meer et al. 2022; Borst & Knies 2023; Johari et al. 2019). The challenges of captivating and retaining seems especially true for employees from more recent generations—or at least of younger age (Schröder 2023)—that are argued to have different and more pronounced expectations and preferences relating to work (Waworuntu et al. 2022). In the Netherlands, for example, the translated ‘captivate and bind’ programs sprout throughout the public sector in an alarmed effort to retain (junior) public servants (Binnenlands Bestuur 2024). However, our knowledge regarding intrinsic motivation amidst bureaucratic constraints falls short on two major accounts. Firstly, insight is lacking on whether a lack of intrinsic motivation is an issue in the public sector as a result of bureaucratic constraints and through what mechanisms this would or would not occur. On the one hand, bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization arguably have several negative effects that relate to a lack of intrinsic motivation (Giauque et al. 2012; George et al. 2021; Lavigna 2013; Serhan et al. 2018). On the other hand, such bureaucratic constraints might not lead to amotivation as public servants’ motivation is argued to be a relatively stable concept (Baldwin 1990; Houtgraaf & Ropes in press) and because public servants’ argued idiosyncratic personality may actually lead them to value bureaucratic elements (Leisha & DeHart-Davis 2007; Merton 1940; Bozeman & Rainey 1998). Applying Self-Determination Theory and assessing whether bureaucratic constraints as forms of external locus of control diminish public servants’ sense of autonomy and competence and thereby lead to amotivation (Ryan & Deci 2000, see also Ekval 1996) would provide insight on underlying mechanisms but has not been applied. Secondly, insight is lacking on the role of age/generation, despite evidence pointing towards a significant moderating function. Millennials and more recent generations are argued to assign particular value to elements of autonomy and positive hierarchical feedback relating to competence in their work (Waworuntu et al. 2022), which appears at odds with bureaucratic constraints such as formalization and centralization typically present in the public sector that may stifle such senses of autonomy and competence (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000; Ekval 1996). Moreover, recent findings dispute that such differences relating to work motivation and preferences are a result of generational differences but a function of age (Schröder 2023). In short, insight is lacking on whether and why bureaucratic constraints relate to amotivation, what role age/generation plays and thus what strategies and tactics to employ in order to captivate and retain public servants—especially junior ones. Therefore, the goal of this study was to scrutinize whether and how bureaucratic dimensions relate to public servants’ intrinsic motivation whilst paying particular attention to self-determination as an underlying mechanism and the role of age. To these ends, several analyses are conducted on cross-sectional data from 1158 public servants working in a range of Dutch public sector organizations to answer the research question: ‘Through which mechanisms do levels of public servants’ intrinsic motivation correlate with the presence of bureaucratic dimensions, taking into account age?’. Scrutinizing these mechanisms allowed for detailed insights in mechanisms of intrinsic motivation and how to safeguard it in the public sector context, especially among specific age groups. The ensuing results provide public sector practitioners, managers, HR-departments and training organizations with avenues on whether and how to effectively counter adverse effects of bureaucratic dimensions on public servants’ motivation in order to captivate and retain public servants’ and in turn improve their performance, wellbeing and sustainable employment. MOTIVATION AMIDST BUREAUCRATIC CONSTRAINTS Intrinsic motivation and Self-Determination Theory Intrinsic motivation encompasses an experience of enjoyment, interest and satisfaction in work that stems from the employee itself, instead of external factors (Wright 2004; Ryan & Deci 2000; Li et al. 2015). According to Self-Determination Theory, the central characteristic of intrinsic motivation is that it stems from an internal locus of control whereby the individual experiences a control over its own actions and outcomes, instead of an external locus of control whereby the individual experiences that its actions and outcomes are determined by external factors such as managers or rules (Deci & Ryan 1985; Li et al. 2015). In more detail, according to Self-Determination Theory, senses of autonomy, competence and relatedness are essential psychological needs that can be satisfied or frustrated and thus determine the degree of an internal locus of control and experience of intrinsic motivation: the individual has to perceive itself as an autonomous actor that is able and capable of acting in correspondence with its values and goals (Chen et al. 2015; Deci & Ryan 1985). External locus of control, however, may lead to a lack of perceived internal locus of control, hampering intrinsic motivation (Bénabou & Tirole 2003; Deci and Ryan 1985) and leading to amotivation whereby the enjoyment, interest and satisfaction of work becomes increasingly absent (Howard et al., 2016). In general, intrinsic motivation is perceived as beneficial for performance and well-being (Houtgraaf & Ropes in press; Ryan & Deci 2000; Grant 2008; Becchetti et al. 2013), which results in the reasoning that an impairing external locus of control that may hamper employees’ intrinsic motivation ought to be avoided. When assessing intrinsic motivation, it is important to determine whether the concept is approached as an attitude or a state, depending on the goal and timeline of assessment. If considered an attitude, intrinsic motivation is assessed based on an individual’s recall over a longer period of time based on the remembering-self, thereby leading to a more average and stable assessment of the level of intrinsic motivation, whereas if considered a state, intrinsic motivation is assessed on based on an individual’s experience in the current moment based on the experiencing-self, thereby leading to accurate but momentarily and fluctuating assessments of levels of intrinsic motivation (Kahneman & Riis 2005). As the goal of this study concerns assessing how individuals recall their work contexts and attitudes in general and on average in order to assess relations, intrinsic motivation is approached and measured as an attitude in this study (Lee & Choi 2003). Formalization as external locus of control Formalization—the degree to which work related processes and interactions are generally governed by formal rules, standard policies and procedures (Boyne 2002; Bozeman 2000)—can be perceived as representing external locus of control that may hamper public servants’ intrinsic motivation. Formalization is a typical bureaucratic dimension of mechanistic organizations (Brown 2014) and although public sector reforms have aimed at reduction of formalization (Van Thiel 2001), public sector organizations are characterized as featuring at least certain levels of formalization (Borins 2010; Boyne 2002; Boye et al. 2022; Houtgraaf et al. 2023). The object of such bureaucratic principles as expressed in formalization is to achieve stability, standardization and to avoid flexibility and change (Ekval 1996) by controlling employee behavior (Hirst et al. 2009). As such, formalization is a clear example of external locus of control that may hamper intrinsic motivation. Arguably, the underlying mechanisms are twofold. On the one hand, the rules and procedures imposed by formalization may frustrate a sense of autonomy as the individual might not be able to act as it would without these external controls (Hirst et al. 2009). On the other hand, formalization its rules and procedures are related to passive, rule-bound and anxious behavior to stay inside established boundaries (Ekval 1996), which may frustrate a sense of competence as the individual might feel less capable and efficacious in conducting work as a result of the external controls (Au 2015). items.title: Rethinking Annotator Simulation: Realistic Evaluation of Whole-Body PET Lesion Interactive Segmentation Methods
items.abstract: Interactive segmentation plays a crucial role in accelerating the annotation, particularly in domains requiring specialized expertise such as nuclear medicine. For example, annotating lesions in whole-body Positron Emission Tomography (PET) images can require over an hour per volume. While previous works evaluate interactive segmentation models through either real user studies or simulated annotators, both approaches present challenges. Real user studies are expensive and often limited in scale, while simulated annotators, also known as robot users, tend to overestimate model performance due to their idealized nature. To address these limitations, we introduce four evaluation metrics that quantify the user shift between real and simulated annotators. In an initial user study involving four annotators, we assess existing robot users using our proposed metrics and find that robot users significantly deviate in performance and annotation behavior compared to real annotators. Based on these findings, we propose a more realistic robot user that reduces the user shift by incorporating human factors such as click variation and inter-annotator disagreement. We validate our robot user in a second user study, involving four other annotators, and show it consistently reduces the simulated-to-real user shift compared to traditional robot users. By employing our robot user, we can conduct more large-scale and cost-efficient evaluations of interactive segmentation models, while preserving the fidelity of real user studies. Our implementation is based on MONAI Label and will be made publicly available.
